diameter region of the lunar surface was modified by a gas release event about a million years ago.
Phases
The Moon rotates, as it orbits Earth, changing orientation toward the Sun, experiencing a lunar day. A lunar day is
equal to one lunar month (one synodic orbit around Earth). The changing position of the illumination of the Moon by the
Sun during a lunar day is observable from Earth as the changing <color=#3366CC>lunar phases</color>. The phases of the moon follow a
repeating cycle, with its starting point at new moon. In the first half of the cycle, the sequence is new moon, crescent,
quarter, gibbous, and full moon. In the second half of the cycle, the sequence is reversed, then the cycle repeats.
The brightness and apparent size of the Moon changes also due to its elliptic orbit around Earth. Consequently, given
the same phase, the Moon's brightness also varies by up to 30% between apogee and perigee. At <color=#3366CC>perigee</color> (closest),
since the Moon is up to 14% closer to Earth than at <color=#3366CC>apogee</color> (most distant), it subtends a <color=#3366CC>solid angle</color> which is up to 30%
larger. A full (or new) moon at such a position is called a <color=#3366CC>supermoon</color>.
Each of the four intermediate phases of the Moon lasts, on average, about seven days (approximately 7.38 days), but
this duration can vary by about ±11% due to the change in the distance between the Moon and Earth between apogee
(farthest point) and perigee (closest point).
The number of days since the most recent new moon is called the Moon's age. A complete cycle of lunar phases is
known as a lunation.
The approximate age and phase of the Moon for any date can be calculated by determining the number of days since a
known new moon (e.g., January 1, 1900, or August 11, 1999) and dividing that value by the average length of a
synodic month (29.53059 days). The remainder of the division represents the Moon's age. This method assumes a
perfectly circular orbit and does not consider the exact time of the new moon, so results may be off by a few hours.
Accuracy decreases as the date moves away from the reference date. This simplified calculation is suitable for many
purposes, but more precise applications require more complex calculation.
True albedo and color of the surface
The Moon's appearance is shaped by its reflective properties and surface composition. Its <color=#3366CC>albedo</color> is about 0.12,
comparable to worn <color=#3366CC>asphalt</color>, making it relatively dark despite its brightness in the night sky. This low albedo represents
the reflectance of the lunar regolith, a layer of fine rock fragments created by meteorite impacts. Light scattering by the
regolith causes the Moon to appear much brighter at full moon than at quarter phases. The Moon also exhibits
retro-reflection, scattering light back toward its source and creating a uniform brightness across its disc without
significant limb darkening.
The Moon's true color, without atmospheric effects, is a muted brownish-gray. This results from silicate minerals in the
regolith, with darker basaltic plains (maria) and lighter feldspar-rich highlands. The maria, formed by ancient volcanic
flows, contain more iron and titanium, giving them a darker tone.
From Earth, the Moon's color can be altered by the atmosphere, at times appearing red or blue. It may appear red
during a <color=#3366CC>lunar eclipse</color>, because of the red spectrum of the Sun's light being <color=#3366CC>refracted</color> onto the Moon by Earth's
atmosphere. Because of this red color, lunar eclipses are also sometimes called blood moons. The Moon can also
seem red when it appears at low angles and through a thick atmosphere. The Moon may also appear blue depending
on the presence of certain particles in the air, such as volcanic particles. Because the words "red moon" and "blue
moon" can also be used to refer to specific <color=#3366CC>full moons</color> of the year, they do not always refer to the presence of red or
blue moonlight.
Eclipses
Eclipses only occur when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are all in a straight line (termed "syzygy"). <color=#3366CC>Solar eclipses</color> occur at
<color=#3366CC>new moon</color>, when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. In contrast, <color=#3366CC>lunar eclipses</color> occur at full moon, when Earth is
between the Sun and Moon. The apparent size of the Moon is roughly the same as that of the Sun, with both being
viewed at close to one-half a degree wide. The Sun is much larger than the Moon, but it is the vastly greater distance
that gives it the same apparent size as the much closer and much smaller Moon from the perspective of Earth. The
variations in apparent size, due to the non-circular orbits, are nearly the same as well, though occurring in different
cycles. This makes possible both <color=#3366CC>total</color> (with the Moon appearing larger than the Sun) and <color=#3366CC>annular</color> (with the Moon
appearing smaller than the Sun) solar eclipses. In a total eclipse, the Moon completely covers the disc of the Sun and
the <color=#3366CC>solar corona</color> becomes visible to the naked eye.
Because the distance between the Moon and Earth is very slowly increasing over time, the angular diameter of the
Moon is decreasing. As the Sun evolves toward becoming a <color=#3366CC>red giant</color>, its size and its apparent diameter in the sky are
slowly increasing. The combination of these two changes means that hundreds of millions of years ago, the Moon
would always completely cover the Sun on solar eclipses, and no annular eclipses were possible. Likewise, hundreds
of millions of years in the future, the Moon will no longer cover the Sun completely, and total solar eclipses will not
occur.
As the Moon's orbit around Earth is inclined by about 5.145° (5° 9) to the <color=#3366CC>orbit of Earth around the Sun</color>, eclipses do not
occur at every full and new moon. For an eclipse to occur, the Moon must be near the intersection of the two orbital
planes. The periodicity and recurrence of eclipses of the Sun by the Moon, and of the Moon by Earth, is described by
the <color=#3366CC>saros</color>, which has a period of approximately 18 years.
Because the Moon continuously blocks the view of a half-degree-wide circular area of the sky, the related phenomenon
of <color=#3366CC>occultation</color> occurs when a bright star or planet passes behind the Moon and is occulted: hidden from view. In this
way, a solar eclipse is an occultation of the Sun. Because the Moon is comparatively close to Earth, occultations of
individual stars are not visible everywhere on the planet, nor at the same time. Because of the <color=#3366CC>precession</color> of the lunar
orbit, each year different stars are occulted.
History of scientific understanding and exploration
Pre-telescopic observation (before 1609)
It is believed by some that the oldest <color=#3366CC>cave paintings</color> from up to 40,000 BP of bulls and geometric shapes, or 20–30,000
year old tally sticks were used to observe the phases of the Moon, keeping time using the waxing and waning of <color=#3366CC>the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Moon's phases</color>. Aspects of the Moon were identified and aggregated in <color=#3366CC>lunar deities</color> from <color=#3366CC>prehistoric times</color> and were
eventually documented and put into symbols from the very first instances of <color=#3366CC>writing</color> in the 4th millennium BC. One of
the earliest-discovered possible depictions of the Moon is a 3,000 BCE rock carving Orthostat 47 at Knowth, Ireland.
The crescent depicting the Moon as with the lunar deity Nanna/Sin have been found from the 3rd millennium BCE.
The oldest named astronomer and poet <color=#3366CC>Enheduanna</color>, <color=#3366CC>Akkadian</color> high priestess to the lunar deity Nanna/Sin and
princess, daughter of <color=#3366CC>Sargon the Great</color> (c. 2334 – c. 2279 BCE), had the Moon tracked in her chambers. The oldest
found and identified depiction of the Moon in an astronomical relation to other astronomical features is the Nebra sky
disc from c. 1800–1600 BCE, depicting features like the <color=#3366CC>Pleiades</color> next to the Moon.
The <color=#3366CC>ancient Greek</color> philosopher <color=#3366CC>Anaxagoras</color> (d. 428 BC) reasoned that the Sun and Moon were both giant spherical
rocks, and that the latter reflected the light of the former. Elsewhere in the 5th century BC to 4th century BC,
Babylonian astronomers had recorded the 18-year <color=#3366CC>Saros cycle</color> of <color=#3366CC>lunar eclipses</color>, and Indian astronomers had
described the Moon's monthly elongation. The Chinese astronomer Shi Shen (fl. 4th century BC) gave instructions for
predicting solar and lunar eclipses.
In <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>'s (384–322 BC) description of the universe, the Moon marked the boundary between the spheres of the
mutable elements (earth, water, air and fire), and the imperishable stars of aether, an influential philosophy that would
dominate for centuries. <color=#3366CC>Archimedes</color> (287–212 BC) designed a planetarium that could calculate the motions of the Moon
and other objects in the Solar System. In the 2nd century BC, Seleucus of Seleucia correctly thought that <color=#3366CC>tides</color> were
due to the attraction of the Moon, and that their height depends on the Moon's position relative to the <color=#3366CC>Sun</color>. In the same
century, Aristarchus computed the size and distance of the Moon from Earth, obtaining a value of about twenty times
the radius of Earth for the distance.
The Chinese of the <color=#3366CC>Han dynasty</color> believed the Moon to be energy equated to <color=#3366CC>qi</color> and their 'radiating influence' theory
recognized that the light of the Moon was merely a reflection of the Sun; Jing Fang (78–37 BC) noted the sphericity of
the Moon. <color=#3366CC>Ptolemy</color> (90–168 AD) greatly improved on the numbers of Aristarchus, calculating a mean distance of 59
times Earth's radius and a diameter of 0.292 Earth diameters, close to the correct values of about 60 and 0.273
respectively. In the 2nd century AD, <color=#3366CC>Lucian</color> wrote the novel <color=#3366CC>A True Story</color>, in which the heroes travel to the Moon and
meet its inhabitants. In 510 AD, the Indian astronomer <color=#3366CC>Aryabhata</color> mentioned in his Aryabhatiya that reflected sunlight is
the cause of the shining of the Moon. The astronomer and physicist <color=#3366CC>Ibn al-Haytham</color> (965–1039) found that <color=#3366CC>sunlight</color> was
not reflected from the Moon like a mirror, but that light was emitted from every part of the Moon's sunlit surface in all
directions. <color=#3366CC>Shen Kuo</color> (1031–1095) of the <color=#3366CC>Song dynasty</color> created an allegory equating the waxing and waning of the
Moon to a round ball of reflective silver that, when doused with white powder and viewed from the side, would appear
to be a crescent. During the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>, before the invention of the telescope, the Moon was increasingly recognized
as a sphere, though many believed that it was "perfectly smooth".
Telescopic exploration (1609–1959)
The <color=#3366CC>telescope</color> was developed and reported on in 1608. The first record of telescopic astronomy and rough mapping of
the Moon's features is from early summer 1609 by Thomas Harriot, but which he did not publish. At the same time
<color=#3366CC>Galileo Galilei</color> too started to use telescopes to observe the sky and the Moon, recording later that year more detailed
observations and crucial conclusions, such as that the Moon was not smooth, featuring mountains and craters, which
he published in 1610 in his ground-breaking and soon widely discussed book Sidereus Nuncius.
Later in the 17th century, the efforts of Giovanni Battista Riccioli and Francesco Maria Grimaldi led to the system of
naming of lunar features in use today. The more exact 1834–1836 Mappa Selenographica of Wilhelm Beer and Johann
Heinrich von Mädler, and their associated 1837 book Der Mond, the first <color=#3366CC>trigonometrically</color> accurate study of lunar
features, included the heights of more than a thousand mountains, and introduced the study of the Moon at accuracies
possible in earthly geography. Lunar craters, first noted by Galileo, were thought to be <color=#3366CC>volcanic</color> until the 1870s proposal
of Richard Proctor that they were formed by collisions. This view gained support in 1892 from the experimentation of
geologist Grove Karl Gilbert, and from comparative studies from 1920 to the 1940s, leading to the development of lunar
stratigraphy, which by the 1950s was becoming a new and growing branch of astrogeology.
First missions to the Moon (1959–1976)
After <color=#3366CC>World War II</color> the first <color=#3366CC>launch systems</color> were developed and by the end of the 1950s they reached capabilities that

allowed the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> and the <color=#3366CC>United States</color> to launch <color=#3366CC>spacecraft</color> into space. The <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color> fueled a closely followed
development of launch systems by the two states, resulting in the so-called <color=#3366CC>Space Race</color> and its later phase the Moon
Race, accelerating efforts and interest in <color=#3366CC>exploration of the Moon</color>.
After the first spaceflight of <color=#3366CC>Sputnik 1</color> in 1957 during International Geophysical Year the spacecraft of the Soviet Union's
Luna program were the first to accomplish a number of goals. Following three unnamed failed missions in 1958, the
first human-made object Luna 1 escaped Earth's gravity and passed the Moon on 4 January 1959. Later that year the
first human-made object <color=#3366CC>Luna 2</color> reached the Moon's surface by intentionally impacting. By the end of the year <color=#3366CC>Luna 3</color>
reached as the first human-made object the normally occluded <color=#3366CC>far side of the Moon</color>, taking the first photographs of it.
The first spacecraft to perform a successful lunar soft landing was <color=#3366CC>Luna 9</color> and the first vehicle to orbit the Moon was
Luna 10, both in 1966.
Following President <color=#3366CC>John F. Kennedy</color>'s 1961 commitment to a crewed Moon landing before the end of the decade, the
United States, under NASA leadership, launched a series of uncrewed probes to develop an understanding of the lunar
surface in preparation for human missions: the Jet Propulsion Laboratory's Ranger program, the Lunar Orbiter program
and the Surveyor program. The crewed <color=#3366CC>Apollo program</color> was developed in parallel; after a series of uncrewed and
crewed tests of the Apollo spacecraft in Earth orbit, and spurred on by a potential Soviet lunar human landing, in 1968
Apollo 8 made the first human mission to lunar orbit (the first Earthlings, two tortoises, had circled the Moon three
months earlier on the Soviet Union's Zond 5, followed by turtles on Zond 6).
The first time a person landed on the Moon and any extraterrestrial body was when <color=#3366CC>Neil Armstrong</color>, the commander of
the American mission <color=#3366CC>Apollo 11</color>, set foot on the Moon at 02:56 UTC on July 21, 1969. Considered the culmination of
the <color=#3366CC>Space Race</color>, an estimated 500 million people worldwide watched the transmission by the Apollo TV camera, the
largest television audience for a live broadcast at that time. While at the same time another mission, the robotic sample
return mission Luna 15 by the Soviet Union had been in orbit around the Moon, becoming together with Apollo 11 the
first ever case of two extraterrestrial missions being conducted at the same time.
The Apollo missions 11 to 17 (except Apollo 13, which aborted its planned lunar landing) removed 837.87 lb of lunar
rock and soil in 2,196 separate samples. Scientific instrument packages were installed on the lunar surface during all
the Apollo landings. Long-lived instrument stations, including heat flow probes, <color=#3366CC>seismometers</color>, and magnetometers,
were installed at the Apollo 12, 14, 15, 16, and 17 landing sites. Direct transmission of data to Earth concluded in late
1977 because of budgetary considerations, but as the stations' lunar laser ranging corner-cube retroreflector arrays are
passive instruments, they are still being used. Apollo 17 in 1972 was the last crewed mission to the Moon's orbit or
surface, and the last to the Moon's vicinity until the Artemis II lunar flyby in 2026. Explorer 49 in 1973 was the last
dedicated U.S. lunar probe until 1994.
The Soviet Union continued sending robotic missions to the Moon until 1976, deploying in 1970 with Luna 17 the first
remote controlled <color=#3366CC>rover</color> <color=#3366CC>Lunokhod 1</color> on an extraterrestrial surface, and collecting and returning 0.3 kg of rock and soil
samples with three Luna sample return missions (Luna 16 in 1970, Luna 20 in 1972, and Luna 24 in 1976).
Moon Treaty and explorational absence (1976–1990)
Following the last Soviet mission to the Moon of 1976, there was little further lunar exploration for fourteen years.
Astronautics had shifted its focus towards the exploration of the <color=#3366CC>inner</color> (e.g. Venera program) and <color=#3366CC>outer</color> (e.g. <color=#3366CC>Pioneer 10</color>,
1972) <color=#3366CC>Solar System</color> <color=#3366CC>planets</color>, but also towards Earth orbit, developing and continuously operating, beside
<color=#3366CC>communication satellites</color>, Earth observation satellites (e.g. Landsat program, 1972), <color=#3366CC>space telescopes</color> and particularly
<color=#3366CC>space stations</color> (e.g. Salyut program, 1971).
Negotiation in 1979 of Moon treaty, and its subsequent ratification in 1984 was the only major activity regarding the
Moon until 1990.
Renewed exploration (1990–present)
In 1990 Hiten – Hagoromo, the first dedicated lunar mission since 1976, reached the Moon's orbit. Sent by Japan, it
became the first lunar mission that was not a Soviet Union or U.S. mission.
In 1994, the U.S. dedicated a mission to fly a spacecraft (Clementine) to the Moon again for the first time since 1973.
This mission obtained the first near-global topographic map of the Moon, and the first global multispectral images of the
lunar surface. In 1998, this was followed by the Lunar Prospector mission, whose instruments indicated the presence of
excess hydrogen at the lunar poles, which is likely to have been caused by the presence of water ice in the upper few
meters of the regolith within permanently shadowed craters.
The next years saw a row of first missions to the Moon by a new group of states actively exploring the Moon. Between
2004 and 2006 the first spacecraft by the <color=#3366CC>European Space Agency</color> (ESA) (SMART-1) orbited the Moon, recording the
first detailed survey of chemical elements on the lunar surface. The <color=#3366CC>Chinese Lunar Exploration Program</color> reached the
Moon for the first time with the orbiter Chang'e 1 (2007–2009), obtaining a full image map of the Moon. <color=#3366CC>India</color> reached,
orbited, and impacted the Moon in 2008 for the first time with its Chandrayaan-1 and Moon Impact Probe, becoming the
fifth and sixth state to do so, creating a high-resolution chemical, mineralogical and photo-geological map of the lunar
surface, and confirming the presence of water molecules in lunar soil.
The U.S. launched the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and the LCROSS impactor on June 18, 2009. LCROSS
completed its mission by making a planned and widely observed impact in the crater Cabeus on October 9, 2009,
whereas LRO is currently in operation, obtaining precise lunar <color=#3366CC>altimetry</color> and high-resolution imagery.
China continued its lunar program in 2010 with Chang'e 2, mapping the surface at a higher resolution over an
eight-month period, and in 2013 with Chang'e 3, a lunar lander along with a <color=#3366CC>lunar rover</color> named Yutu. This was the first
lunar rover mission since Lunokhod 2 in 1973 and the first lunar soft landing since Luna 24 in 1976, making China the
third country to achieve this.
In 2014 the first privately funded probe, the Manfred Memorial Moon Mission, flew by the Moon. Another Chinese rover
mission, Chang'e 4, achieved the first landing on <color=#3366CC>the Moon's far side</color> in early 2019. Also in 2019, India successfully sent
its second probe, Chandrayaan-2, to the Moon. In 2020, China carried out its first robotic sample return mission
(Chang'e 5), bringing back 1,731 grams of lunar material to Earth.
The U.S. developed plans for returning astronauts to the Moon beginning in 2004, and with the signing of the U.S.-led
Artemis Accords in 2020, the Artemis program aims to return humans to the Moon in the 2020s. The Accords have
been joined by a growing number of countries. The introduction of the Artemis Accords has fueled a renewed
discussion about the international framework and cooperation of lunar activity, building on the Moon Treaty and the
ESA-led Moon Village concept.
In 2022, South Korea launched Danuri successfully, its first lunar probe, from the US. In 2023 and 2024, India and
Japan became the fourth and fifth country to soft land a spacecraft on the Moon, following the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> and United
States in the 1960s, and China in 2013. Notably, Japan's spacecraft, the Smart Lander for Investigating Moon, survived
three lunar nights. In February 2024, the IM-1 lander became the first commercially built lander to land on the Moon.
China launched Chang'e 6 in May 2024, which conducted the first sample return from the <color=#3366CC>far side of the Moon</color>. It also
carried a Chinese rover to conduct <color=#3366CC>infrared spectroscopy</color> of lunar surface. <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color> sent a lunar orbiter called ICUBE-Q
along with Chang'e 6. Nova-C 2, iSpace Lander and Blue Ghost were all launched to the Moon in 2024.
NASA's Artemis II crewed lunar flyby mission launched in April 2026. It was the first crewed mission around the Moon
since the Apollo era. Christina Koch became the first woman, Victor Glover the first person of color, Canadian Jeremy
Hansen the first non-American, and commander Reid Wiseman the oldest person, to leave <color=#3366CC>low Earth orbit</color> and to fly
around the Moon.
Future
Both the U.S. and Chinese lunar programs have the goal to establish a lunar base in the 2030s with their international
partners, being the first crewed lunar landings since Apollo 17 in 1972.
Following the Artemis III test flight in <color=#3366CC>low Earth orbit</color> scheduled for 2027, NASA plans to return humans to the lunar
surface in 2028, with two Artemis IV astronauts landing on the lunar south pole. While the Apollo missions were
explorational in nature, the Artemis program plans to establish a more permanent presence. To this end, the U.S. is
partnering with industry for lunar communications, payload delivery, and in situ resource utilization through programs
such as NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services, and DARPA lunar programs.
China is continuing its ambitious <color=#3366CC>Chang'e program</color>, having announced joint missions with Russia's struggling
Luna-Glob program. Two lunar survey missions are planned, Chang'e 7 in 2026 and Chang'e 8 in 2028, before a
crewed landing in 2029 or 2030.
Human interaction and presence
The first extraterrestrial probes reached the Moon (Luna program) in 1959, just a year into the space age, after the first
ever orbital flight. Since then, humans have sent a range of probes and people to the Moon. The first stay of people on
the Moon was conducted in 1969, in a series of crewed exploration missions (the <color=#3366CC>Apollo Program</color>), the last having
taken place in 1972.
Uninterrupted presence has been the case through the remains of impactors, landings and lunar orbiters. Some
landings and orbiters have maintained a small lunar infrastructure, providing continuous observation and
communication at the Moon. Longterm missions continuing to be active are some orbiters such as the 2009-launched
Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter surveilling the Moon for future missions, as well as some Landers such as the
2013-launched Chang'e 3 with its Lunar Ultraviolet Telescope still operational. Five retroreflectors have been installed
on the Moon since the 1970s and since used for accurate measurements of the physical <color=#3366CC>librations</color> through laser
ranging to the Moon.
Increasing human activity in <color=#3366CC>cislunar space</color> as well as on the Moon's surface, particularly missions at the far side of the
Moon or the lunar north and <color=#3366CC>south polar</color> regions, are in need for a lunar infrastructure. For that purpose, orbiters in
orbits around the Moon or the Earth–Moon Lagrange points, have since 2006 been operated. With highly <color=#3366CC>eccentric</color>
<color=#3366CC>orbits</color> providing continuous communication, as with the orbit of Queqiao and Queqiao-2 relay satellite.
There are several missions by different agencies and companies planned to establish a long-term human presence on
the Moon, with the Artemis program as the currently most advanced program.
Human impact
While the Moon has the lowest planetary protection target-categorization, its degradation as a pristine body and
scientific place has been discussed. If there is astronomy performed from the Moon, it will need to be free from any
physical and <color=#3366CC>radio pollution</color>. While the Moon has no significant atmosphere, traffic and impacts on the Moon causes
clouds of dust that can spread far and possibly contaminate the original state of the Moon and its special scientific
content. Scholar Alice Gorman asserts that, although the Moon is inhospitable, describing the Moon as dead negates
its dynamics, which requires sustainable human activity to treat the Moon's ecology as a co-participant.
The so-called "Tardigrade affair" of the 2019 crashed Beresheet lander and its carrying of <color=#3366CC>tardigrades</color> has been
discussed as an example for lacking measures and lacking international regulation for planetary protection.
Space debris beyond Earth around the Moon has been considered as a future challenge with increasing numbers of
missions to the Moon, particularly as a danger for such missions. As such lunar waste management has been raised as
an issue which future lunar missions, particularly on the surface, need to tackle.
Human remains have been transported to the Moon, including by private companies such as Celestis and Elysium
Space. Because the Moon has been sacred or significant to many cultures, the practice of space burials have attracted
criticism from <color=#3366CC>indigenous peoples</color> leaders. For example, then<color=#3366CC>Navajo Nation</color> president Albert Hale criticized NASA for
sending the <color=#3366CC>cremated</color> ashes of scientist Eugene Shoemaker to the Moon in 1998.
Beside the remains of human activity on the Moon, there have been some intended permanent installations like the
Moon Museum art piece, Apollo 11 goodwill messages, six lunar plaques, the Fallen Astronaut memorial, and other
artifacts.
Astronomy from the Moon
The Moon has been used as a site for astronomical and Earth observations. The Earth appears in the Moon's sky with
an <color=#3366CC>apparent size</color> of 1° 48 to 2°, three to four times the size of the Moon or Sun in Earth's sky, or about the apparent
width of two little fingers at an arm's length away. Observations from the Moon started as early as 1966 with the first
images of Earth from the Moon, taken by Lunar Orbiter 1. Of particular cultural significance is the 1968 photograph
called <color=#3366CC>Earthrise</color>, taken by <color=#3366CC>Bill Anders</color> of Apollo 8 in 1968. In April 1972 the Apollo 16 mission set up the first dedicated
telescope, the Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph, recording various astronomical photos and spectra.
The Moon is recognized as an excellent site for telescopes. It is relatively nearby; certain craters near the poles are
permanently dark and cold and especially useful for <color=#3366CC>infrared telescopes</color>; and <color=#3366CC>radio telescopes</color> on the far side would be
shielded from the radio chatter of Earth. The lunar soil, although it poses a problem for any moving parts of <color=#3366CC>telescopes</color>,
can be mixed with <color=#3366CC>carbon nanotubes</color> and <color=#3366CC>epoxies</color> and employed in the construction of mirrors up to 50 meters in
diameter. A lunar zenith telescope can be made cheaply with an ionic liquid.
With increased human activity on the surface of the Moon the atmospheric circulation of lunar dust will increase,
reducing the favorable conditions for astronomy from the surface depending on measures to mitigate the spread of
lunar dust.
Living on the Moon
Humans have lived on the Moon in groups of two and for up to three days. Altogether twelve people have stayed on the
Moon over the course of six visits. They all lived in one type of surface habitat, the Apollo Lunar Module. In the course
of these stays some people have spent in total up to one day roaming the surface.
Challenges when roaming the surface arise from lunar dust sticking to suits and tools, and has been carried inside the
habitats. Astronauts could taste and smell the dust, which smells like gunpowder and was called the "Apollo aroma".
This fine lunar dust can cause health issues.
In 2019, at least one plant seed sprouted in an experiment on the Chang'e 4 lander. It was carried from Earth along
with other small life in its Lunar Micro Ecosystem.
Legal status
Although Luna landers scattered pennants of the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> on the Moon, and U.S. flags were symbolically planted
at their landing sites by the Apollo astronauts, no nation claims ownership of any part of the Moon's surface. Likewise
no private ownership of parts of the Moon, or as a whole, is considered credible.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty defines the Moon and all outer space as the "province of all mankind". It restricts the use
of the Moon to peaceful purposes, explicitly banning military installations and <color=#3366CC>weapons of mass destruction</color>. A majority
of countries are parties of this treaty. The 1979 Moon Agreement was created to elaborate, and restrict the exploitation
of the Moon's resources by any single nation, leaving it to a yet unspecified international regulatory regime. As of
January 2020, it has been signed and ratified by 18 nations, none of which have human spaceflight capabilities.
Since 2020, countries have joined the U.S. in their Artemis Accords, which are challenging the treaty. The U.S. has
furthermore emphasized in a presidential executive order ("Encouraging International Support for the Recovery and
Use of Space Resources.") that "the United States does not view outer space as a 'global commons and calls the Moon
Agreement "a failed attempt at constraining free enterprise".
With Australia signing and ratifying both the Moon Treaty in 1986 as well as the Artemis Accords in 2020, there has
been a discussion if they can be harmonized. In this light an Implementation Agreement for the Moon Treaty has been
advocated for, as a way to compensate for the shortcomings of the Moon Treaty and to harmonize it with other laws
and agreements such as the Artemis Accords, allowing it to be more widely accepted.
In the face of such increasing commercial and national interest, particularly prospecting territories, U.S. lawmakers
have introduced in late 2020 specific regulation for the conservation of historic landing sites and interest groups have
argued for making such sites <color=#3366CC>World Heritage Sites</color> and zones of scientific value protected zones, all of which add to the
legal availability and territorialization of the Moon.
In 2021, the Declaration of the Rights of the Moon was created by a group of "lawyers, space archaeologists and
concerned citizens", drawing on precedents in the Rights of Nature movement and the concept of legal personality for
non-human entities in space.
Coordination and regulation
Increasing human activity at the Moon has raised the need for coordination to safeguard international and commercial
lunar activity. Issues from cooperation to mere coordination, through for example the development of a shared Lunar
time, have been raised.
In particular the establishment of an <color=#3366CC>international</color> or <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color> regulatory regime for lunar human activity has been
called for by the Moon Treaty and suggested through an Implementation Agreement, but remains contentious. Current
lunar programs are multilateral, with the US-led Artemis program and the China-led International Lunar Research
Station. For broader international cooperation and coordination, the International Lunar Exploration Working Group
(ILEWG), the Moon Village Association (MVA) and more generally the International Space Exploration Coordination
Group (ISECG) has been established.
In culture and life
Timekeeping
Since pre-historic times people have taken note of <color=#3366CC>the Moon's phases</color> and its <color=#3366CC>waxing and waning cycle</color> and used it to
keep record of time. Tally sticks, notched bones dating as far back as 20–30,000 years ago, are believed by some to
mark the phases of the Moon. The counting of the days between the Moon's phases eventually gave rise to generalized
time periods of lunar cycles as <color=#3366CC>months</color>, and possibly of its phases as <color=#3366CC>weeks</color>.
The words for the month in a range of different languages carry this relation between the period of the month and the
Moon etymologically. The English month as well as moon, and its cognates in other Indo-European languages (e.g. the
<color=#3366CC>Latin</color> mensis and <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greek</color> (meis) or (mēn), meaning "month") stem from the <color=#3366CC>Proto-Indo-European</color> (PIE) root of
moon, *méh1nōt, derived from the PIE verbal root *meh1-, "to measure", "indicat[ing] a functional conception of the
Moon, i.e. marker of the month" (cf. the English words measure and menstrual). To give another example from a
different <color=#3366CC>language family</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Chinese language</color> uses the same word for moon as for month, which furthermore can be
found in the symbols for the word week.
This lunar timekeeping gave rise to the historically dominant, but varied, <color=#3366CC>lunisolar calendars</color>. The 7th-century <color=#3366CC>Islamic</color>
<color=#3366CC>calendar</color> is an example of a purely <color=#3366CC>lunar calendar</color>, where months are traditionally determined by the visual sighting of
the hilal, or earliest crescent moon, over the horizon.
Of particular significance has been the occasion of <color=#3366CC>full moon</color>, highlighted and celebrated in a range of calendars and
cultures, an example being the Buddhist <color=#3366CC>Vesak</color>. The full moon around the <color=#3366CC>southern</color> or <color=#3366CC>northern autumnal equinox</color> is
often called the <color=#3366CC>harvest moon</color> and is celebrated with festivities such as the <color=#3366CC>Harvest Moon Festival</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Chinese lunar</color>
<color=#3366CC>calendar</color>, its second most important celebration after <color=#3366CC>the Chinese</color> lunisolar <color=#3366CC>Lunar New Year</color>.
Furthermore, association of time with the Moon can also be found in religion, such as the ancient Egyptian temporal
and lunar deity Khonsu.
Cultural representation
Humans have not only observed the Moon since <color=#3366CC>prehistoric times</color>, but have also developed intricate perceptions of the
Moon. Over time the Moon has been characterized and associated in many different ways, from having a <color=#3366CC>spirit</color> or being
<color=#3366CC>a deity</color>, and an aspect thereof or an aspect in astrology, being made an important part of many <color=#3366CC>cosmologies</color>.
This rich history of humans viewing the Moon has been evidenced starting with depictions from 40,000 BP and in
written form from the 4th millennium BCE in the earliest cases of <color=#3366CC>writing</color>. The oldest named astronomer and poet
<color=#3366CC>Enheduanna</color>, <color=#3366CC>Akkadian</color> high priestess to the lunar deity Nanna/Sin and daughter of <color=#3366CC>Sargon the Great</color> (c. 2334 – c.
2279 BCE), tracked the Moon and wrote poems about her divine Moon.
Crescent
For the representation of the Moon, especially its <color=#3366CC>lunar phases</color>, the crescent has been a recurring symbol in a range of
cultures since at least 3,000 BCE or possibly earlier with bull horns dating to the earliest <color=#3366CC>cave paintings</color> at 40,000 BP.
In <color=#3366CC>writing systems</color> such as Chinese the crescent has developed into the symbol, the word for Moon, and in ancient
Egyptian it was the symbol, meaning Moon and spelled like the ancient Egyptian lunar deity Iah, which the other
ancient Egyptian lunar deities Khonsu and <color=#3366CC>Thoth</color> were associated with.
Iconographically the crescent was used in <color=#3366CC>Mesopotamia</color> as the primary symbol of Nanna/Sîn, the ancient <color=#3366CC>Sumerian</color>
lunar deity, who was the father of <color=#3366CC>Inanna/Ishtar</color>, the goddess of the planet <color=#3366CC>Venus</color> (symbolized as the eight pointed Star
of Ishtar), and <color=#3366CC>Utu/Shamash</color>, the god of the Sun (symbolized as a disc, optionally with eight rays), all three often
depicted next to each other. Nanna/Sîn is, like some other lunar deities, for example Iah and Khonsu of ancient Egypt,
Mene/Selene of ancient Greece and Luna of ancient Rome, depicted as a horned deity, featuring crescent shaped
headgears or crowns.
The particular arrangement of the crescent with a star known as the <color=#3366CC>star and crescent</color> goes back to the Bronze Age,
representing either the Sun and Moon, or the Moon and the planet Venus, in combination. It came to represent the
selene goddess <color=#3366CC>Artemis</color>, and via the patronage of Hecate, which as triple deity under the epithet trimorphos/trivia
included aspects of Artemis/Diana, came to be used as a symbol of Byzantium, with <color=#3366CC>Virgin Mary</color> (Queen of Heaven)
later taking her place, becoming depicted in Marian veneration on a crescent and adorned with stars. Since then the
<color=#3366CC>heraldric</color> use of the star and crescent proliferated, Byzantium's symbolism possibly influencing the development of the
Ottoman flag, specifically the combination of the Turkish crescent with a star, and becoming a popular symbol for Islam
(as the of the <color=#3366CC>Islamic calendar</color>) and <color=#3366CC>for a range of nations</color>.
Other associations
The features of the Moon, the contrasting brighter highlands and darker maria, have been seen by different cultures
forming abstract shapes. Such shapes are among others the Man in the Moon (e.g. Coyolxāuhqui) or the Moon Rabbit
(e.g. the Chinese Tu'er Ye or in <color=#3366CC>Indigenous American mythologies</color> the aspect of the Maya moon goddess, from which
possibly Awilix is derived, or of Metztli/Tēcciztēcatl).
Occasionally some lunar deities have been also depicted driving a chariot across the sky, such as the Hindu
<color=#3366CC>Chandra/Soma</color>, the Greek Artemis, which is associated with Selene, or Luna, Selene's ancient Roman equivalent.
Throughout the global Middle Ages, the moon held an important cultural role in topics as wide-ranging as <color=#3366CC>love poetry</color>,
<color=#3366CC>prophecy</color>, medical thinking.
Color and material wise the Moon has been associated in Western <color=#3366CC>alchemy</color> with <color=#3366CC>silver</color>, while gold is associated with
the Sun.
Through a miracle, the so-called splitting of the Moon in <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, association with the Moon applies also to <color=#3366CC>Muhammad</color>.
Representation in modern culture
The perception of the Moon in the <color=#3366CC>modern era</color> has been informed by <color=#3366CC>telescope</color>-enabled <color=#3366CC>modern astronomy</color>. These new
insights inspired cultural references, connecting romantic reflections about the Moon and speculative fiction such as
science-fiction dealing with the Moon.
Later <color=#3366CC>spaceflight</color> ushered in the space age, which produced especially with the first <color=#3366CC>Moon landings</color> historic
achievements and references for <color=#3366CC>global society</color>, represented through images of Earth from a distance and summarized
in an awe and awareness called the overview effect, amounting to Moon joy by reaching the Moon.
This has been accompanied by public and critical reflection on humanity's cultural and legal relation to the celestial
body, particularly as an object of <color=#3366CC>imperialism</color>, as in the <color=#3366CC>space race</color>, and as an object of <color=#3366CC>colonialism</color> through lunar
resources commercialization. The 1970 poem "Whitey on the Moon" has become famous for its expression of such
critical reflections. Other reflections have invoked the Moon's nature, raising issues like lunar conservation and
sustainability, understanding the Moon as a common.
In 2021 the 20 July became the International Moon Day, the date of the <color=#3366CC>first crewed Moon landing</color>.
Lunar effect
The lunar effect is a supposed correlation between specific stages of the roughly 29.5-day lunar cycle, and behavior
and physiological changes in humans on Earth. Lunar cycles have significant impacts on human culture, but no solid
evidence connects these cycles to human biology.
The Moon has long been associated with insanity and irrationality; the words lunacy and lunatic are derived from the
Latin name for the Moon, Luna. Philosophers <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color> and <color=#3366CC>Pliny the Elder</color> argued that the full moon induced insanity in
susceptible individuals, believing that the brain, which is mostly water, must be affected by the Moon and its power over
the tides, but the Moon's gravity is too slight to affect any single person. In modern society lunar effects have been
claimed to be responsible for supposed increased admissions to psychiatric hospitals, traffic accidents, homicides or
suicides during a full moon, but these claims have been invalidated by at least 37 studies.
